title: Our solar system and orbits
examTip: Know what is in our solar system and where it sits in the Milky Way. Know that gravity keeps planets and satellites in circular orbits. Be ready to explain why an orbiting object's velocity changes while its speed stays the same.
introTips: Our solar system has one star, the Sun. Eight planets and the dwarf planets orbit it. Moons orbit the planets.
Gravity provides the force that keeps planets and satellites in their circular orbits.
In a circular orbit the speed stays the same, but the velocity keeps changing, because the direction changes.
intro: The Earth is one of eight planets moving round the Sun. In this lesson you learn what makes up our solar system. You learn how planets, moons and artificial satellites are alike and how they differ. You also learn how gravity keeps them all in orbit.

keyPoints.heading: What is in our solar system
keyPoints.content: Our solar system contains: - one star, the Sun - the eight planets that orbit the Sun - the dwarf planets that orbit the Sun - natural satellites: the moons that orbit planets. Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.
writeBullets: Eight planets and the dwarf planets orbit the Sun
Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy

keyTerms.def: The Sun, plus the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit it, and the moons that orbit the planets
A moon: a natural object that orbits a planet
The galaxy that our solar system is a small part of

keyPoints.memTip: One star, eight planets, dwarf planets, moons. All inside the Milky Way.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Check the student knows a moon is a natural satellite. Many think 'satellite' only means a machine.

keyPoints.heading: Planets, moons and artificial satellites
keyPoints.content: Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites to keep moving in their circular orbits. This is true for both natural and artificial satellites. Similarities: - All of them orbit a larger body. - Gravity provides the force that keeps each one in orbit. - Their orbits are close to circular. Distinctions (differences): - Planets orbit the Sun, which is a star. - Moons are natural satellites. They orbit planets. - Artificial satellites are made by people. They are put into orbit, mostly around the Earth.
writeBullets: Gravity provides the force that keeps planets and satellites in circular orbits
Similar: all orbit a larger body, all held by gravity, orbits close to circular
Moons are natural satellites; they orbit planets
Artificial satellites are made by people; mostly orbit the Earth

keyTerms.def: An object made by people and put into orbit, mostly around the Earth
The path of an object moving round a larger body, kept there by gravity

keyPoints.memTip: Planets go round the Sun. Moons go round planets. Artificial satellites are made by us.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Ask the student for one similarity and one difference. This matches how the question is usually asked.

keyPoints.heading: Velocity, speed and stable orbits
keyPoints.content: In a circular orbit, gravity always pulls towards the centre of the orbit. This force is at right angles to the direction of motion. So the force changes the object's direction, but not its speed. Velocity is a vector. It includes direction. The direction keeps changing, so the velocity keeps changing. The speed stays the same. For a stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes. - A faster object needs a smaller orbit, closer in. - A slower object needs a larger orbit, further out. This is why satellites in higher orbits move more slowly.
writeBullets: In a circular orbit, gravity acts towards the centre, at right angles to the motion
Gravity changes the direction but not the speed
Velocity is a vector, so changing direction means changing velocity
Circular orbit: changing velocity, unchanged speed
Stable orbit: if the speed changes, the radius must change
Faster → smaller orbit; slower → larger orbit

keyTerms.def: An orbit that stays the same size; its radius must change if the object's speed changes

keyPoints.memTip: Same speed, new direction, new velocity. Faster = closer in.
keyPoints.tutor_note: If the student says the velocity is constant, ask what happens to the direction. Velocity includes direction.

0.question: What are the moons that orbit planets called?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. Moons are natural satellites. They orbit planets and are part of the solar system.
0.wrongFeedback: Moons are natural satellites. Artificial satellites are made by people. Dwarf planets orbit the Sun.

1.question: What keeps planets, moons and artificial satellites in their orbits?
1.correctFeedback: Correct. Gravity provides the force that keeps planets and satellites in their circular orbits.
1.wrongFeedback: Gravity provides the force that keeps planets and satellites, natural and artificial, in their circular orbits.

2.question: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at a steady speed. What happens to its velocity?
options: It stays the same, because the speed is steady
It changes, because the direction keeps changing
It increases, because gravity speeds it up
2.correctFeedback: Correct. Velocity includes direction. The direction keeps changing, so the velocity changes even though the speed does not.
2.wrongFeedback: Velocity is a vector, so it includes direction. In a circular orbit the direction keeps changing. So the velocity changes, while the speed stays the same.

commonMistakes: Saying a moon is not a satellite. Moons are natural satellites.
Saying velocity is constant in a circular orbit. The speed is constant, but the direction changes, so the velocity changes.
Saying a faster satellite needs a bigger orbit. For a stable orbit, a faster object needs a smaller orbit.
examTips: For 'compare' questions, give at least one similarity and one difference.
To explain changing velocity with unchanged speed, say that gravity acts at right angles to the motion.
Use the word 'gravity' to say what provides the force for an orbit.
revisionCardBullets: Solar system: one star (the Sun), eight planets, dwarf planets, moons
Moons = natural satellites; they orbit planets
Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy
Gravity provides the force for circular orbits of planets and satellites
Artificial satellites are made by people; mostly orbit the Earth
Circular orbit: velocity changes (direction changes), speed unchanged
Stable orbit: if speed changes, radius must change; faster → smaller orbit
